history.heading: Indigenous peoples and conquest
paragraphs: Chile, a long, narrow country between the Andes and the Pacific, was home to peoples such as the Chinchorro, who practised artificial mummification thousands of years before the Egyptians, the Aymara and Atacameño in the north, and the Mapuche in the south. The Inca Empire extended into northern and central Chile. Rapa Nui (Easter Island) developed its own Polynesian culture and the famous moai statues.
Pedro de Valdivia founded Santiago in 1541. The Mapuche fiercely resisted Spanish conquest for over three centuries in the Arauco War, keeping control of territory south of the Biobío River.

history.heading: Independence and the 19th century
paragraphs: Chile began its independence movement in 1810, and Bernardo O'Higgins and José de San Martín secured independence after the Battle of Maipú in 1818. Chile became one of the most stable states in Latin America in the 19th century.

Victory over Peru and Bolivia in the War of the Pacific (1879–1884) gave Chile the nitrate-rich Atacama Desert. In the 1880s the Chilean state occupied Mapuche lands in the south (the "Pacification of Araucanía").

history.heading: Allende and Pinochet
paragraphs: In 1970 Salvador Allende became the first Marxist elected president in Latin America. His government nationalised copper and banks amid economic crisis and polarisation. On 11 September 1973, a military coup led by General Augusto Pinochet overthrew him.

Pinochet's dictatorship killed or disappeared over 3,000 people and tortured tens of thousands, while implementing free-market reforms. A 1988 plebiscite voted him out, and democracy returned in 1990.

history.heading: Democratic Chile
paragraphs: Chile became one of Latin America's most prosperous countries. In 2019 mass protests against inequality led to a process to replace the Pinochet-era constitution, but voters rejected both a left-leaning draft in 2022 and a conservative draft in 2023. A massive earthquake in 2010 was among the strongest ever recorded. In the 2025 presidential election, Chileans elected the right-wing candidate José Antonio Kast.

culture.heading: Poets and music
paragraphs: Chile is called a "land of poets": Gabriela Mistral and Pablo Neruda both won the Nobel Prize in Literature. Isabel Allende is one of the most widely read Spanish-language novelists. The Nueva Canción movement, with Violeta Parra and Víctor Jara, combined folk music with social themes.

Spanish is the main language, spoken with a distinctive Chilean accent and slang. Most Chileans are Catholic, and evangelical churches have grown. Mapuche culture is a growing part of national identity.

culture.heading: Traditions and food
paragraphs: The national dance is the cueca. Independence celebrations, the Fiestas Patrias in September, feature fondas, empanadas and asado. Other foods include pastel de choclo (corn pie), cazuela, seafood and completos (hot dogs). Chile is a major wine producer, and pisco is a national spirit.
Football is the most popular sport; Chile won the Copa América in 2015 and 2016.

politics.heading: Presidential republic
paragraphs: Chile is a presidential republic. The president is elected for a four-year term and cannot serve consecutive terms. The National Congress consists of a Chamber of Deputies and a Senate. Politics features coalitions of left and right, and voters have shown strong swings between them in recent years.
Key debates include pensions, inequality, public security, migration and Mapuche land claims.

politics.heading: Foreign relations
paragraphs: Chile has an open, trade-oriented foreign policy and has signed free trade agreements with most of the world's major economies. It has had territorial disputes with Peru and Bolivia, resolved through the International Court of Justice, and it claims part of Antarctica.

economy.heading: Copper and exports
paragraphs: Chile has one of the most stable and prosperous economies in Latin America. It is the world's largest copper producer, and copper accounts for around half of exports, with state company Codelco and private mines in the Atacama Desert. Chile also has some of the world's largest lithium reserves.
Other exports include fruit (cherries and grapes), salmon, wine and forestry products. China is the largest trading partner. The currency is the Chilean peso.

economy.heading: Challenges
paragraphs: Despite strong growth, Chile has high income inequality, and its private pension system is controversial. Other challenges include dependence on copper prices, water shortages from long droughts, and rising crime. Chile is expanding solar and wind power, especially in the Atacama, and aims to produce green hydrogen.
